taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO. Three accepted varieties are recognized globally; learner stays species-level. Field-key caution (2026-10-19): Kew/POWO currently accepts Phyla nodiflora, P. lanceolata and P. cuneifolia separately. Cardoso et al. (2025), Nordic Journal of Botany doi:10.1002/njb.04825, propose a broader P. nodiflora concept encompassing lanceolata and cuneifolia because leaf differences overlap. Retain the project's current Kew species concepts, but teach leaf traits as typical tendencies, not infallible single-character diagnoses.
look_here_first: CREW FIELD ID: First find a low mat of running stems. Look at nodes for opposite paired leaves, and follow the thin mostly leafless flower stalk back to a leaf axil. Its tiny white/lilac flowers cluster around a purplish button that elongates with age. Inspect 3–5 mature leaves: a blade commonly widest beyond midlength, with most teeth toward the tip and a narrowing, less-toothed base. Rooting at buried/contact nodes is typical but may be hidden. These characters support Phyla; they do NOT unambiguously separate traditional P. nodiflora from P. lanceolata or P. cuneifolia, which a 2025 revision combines.

project_inclusion.range_basis: BONAP/NAPA maps Phyla nodiflora at county level and treats it as native in Texas. Hays County — UT Plant Resources Center's Purola Preserve flora lists P. nodiflora among plants occurring naturally and not introduced. Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center's Travis County Verbenaceae herbarium index includes P. nodiflora; additional wild Travis records are documented at Emma Long and Reimers Ranch. Williamson County — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed county treatment for P. nodiflora.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Frogfruit is widely planted as a groundcover. County proof uses native-flora/herbarium treatments, not landscape plantings.

best_field_traits: GROUND LEVEL: creeping perennial, frequently forming interconnected mats; a growing point may root where it touches soil
NODE: paired opposite (decussate) leaves with little or no visible stalk; young stems can appear nearly four-sided
LEAF: generally spoon-shaped to elliptic; many mature blades broader beyond halfway and toothed mainly nearer tip; check several leaves because this varies
FLOWER: one slender, mostly naked stalk from a leaf axil, topped with a tight button/cylinder of minute white to lavender two-lipped flowers
FRUIT: an older head becomes elongated and scaly; individual dry fruits split into two tiny one-seeded mericarps, not usually visible without dissection
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Phyla lanceolata: The best leaf split: P. nodiflora is usually widest beyond the middle and its teeth are concentrated in the distal half; P. lanceolata is widest nearer the middle and the teeth extend farther down the blade. Phyla cuneifolia: Wedgeleaf frogfruit has a more distinctly wedge-shaped leaf architecture. Use several mature leaves rather than one odd leaf, because Phyla leaf shape varies along a shoot. Glandularia spp.: Glandularia can also form low mats with verbena-like flowers, but its flowers are much larger and borne in more open terminal heads/spikes; Phyla has tiny flowers packed into a compact button/cylinder on a naked axillary peduncle.
crew_20_second_sequence: STEP 1: Find the creeping stem rather than judging one isolated leaf.
STEP 2: Check a node for two opposite leaves and any roots or root buds against the soil.
STEP 3: Trace the narrow flower-head stalk to a leaf axil; look for a densely packed button/cylinder of tiny pale flowers.
STEP 4: Check the tooth pattern and widest point on three to five fully formed leaves, ideally from more than one shoot.
STEP 5: If flower-head attachment is hidden or leaves overlap other Phyla concepts, report Phyla sp. rather than force a precise species.
morphology_keys.habit_and_stems: Perennial clonal, low prostrate to procumbent herb. Tough, flexible runners/rooting stems, typically 2.5–30 cm tall including ascending shoots (UT Williamson County treatment); buried/contact nodes can form adventitious roots. Young shoots may be weakly four-angled. Rooting habit is useful but not species-unique.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Opposite and decussate: two leaves are borne at each node, with successive pairs rotated about 90 degrees. Not alternate; pair attachment is a high-value field check.
morphology_keys.leaves: Usually (5–)10–30 mm long × 3–12 mm wide in UT Williamson County specimens. Oblanceolate, spatulate or elliptic, tapering toward a short petiole (often <2.5 mm). Usually several teeth per side mainly above the middle, but old/shaded/drought shoots vary considerably; inspect multiple leaves. Hairs can be inconspicuous without magnification.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: A single many-flowered condensed headlike spike arises from a leaf axil on a mostly leafless peduncle (usually 4–70 mm, occasionally to 90 mm in UT county treatment). Head initially approximately spherical/button-shaped, elongating into a short cylinder as it matures (often 5–20 × 4.5–8 mm). Repeated purple/green overlapping bracts form a scaly head.
morphology_keys.flowers: Minute white, lilac or pinkish, bilaterally symmetrical, two-lipped flowers, sometimes with yellow throat/marking, emerge in a ring around the head. Treat color as variable; flower architecture and stalk origin matter more.
morphology_keys.fruits: Dry schizocarp hidden among bracts and enclosed by a persistent calyx; separates into TWO one-seeded mericarps (nutlets), usually about 1.6–2 mm long. A photo of the brown cylindrical HEAD does not by itself reveal the isolated mericarps. Hand lens or dissected mature head needed.
morphology_keys.microscope_traits: Appressed two-armed, medifixed (T-shaped or malpighiaceous) hairs are characteristic of Phyla. Check stems and leaf surfaces under magnification; do not claim that ordinary habit photos resolve individual hairs. Genus-level, not a nodiflora-vs-lanceolata shortcut.
morphology_keys.hays_county_habitat: Look in openings, lawns, sidewalk/bed edges, moist low spots, drainage margins, alluvial soils and disturbed ground in Central Texas. The taxon tolerates wet spells and dry periods; its growth and bloom display may change with mowing or irrigation. A planted patch alone is not proof of natural county occurrence.
morphology_keys.phenology: Flowers repeatedly through warm weather in Central Texas, generally spring through fall and sometimes longer in mild conditions; living stems may persist through winter. Heads can carry flowers, bracts and developing fruits together, and the same patch can show rounded young and cylindrical old heads.
morphology_keys.crew_management: Do not confuse low height with an absence of management value: flowering heads offer nectar, and foliage serves as a documented caterpillar host. Repeated close mowing removes blooms. Flag before routine blanket herbicide/weeding on pollinator or restoration sites; tolerate appropriate spread but still manage walkway edges and competing vegetation as site needs dictate.
morphology_keys.larval_host_evidence: Native Plant Society of Texas reports frogfruit as host/nectar plant for Phaon crescent, common buckeye and white peacock butterflies. This is a host-association summary, NOT a local host-species count or verification that all three are breeding at the exact site. Nectar visitors are not automatically larvae.
morphology_keys.when_to_stop_at_genus: Recent revision (Cardoso, O'Leary & Trovó, 2025) recognizes only P. betulifolia and a broad P. nodiflora, synonymizing the traditional P. lanceolata and P. cuneifolia; Kew currently treats these separately. Leaf shape/teeth/texture overlap. When the morphology of an individual plant will not separate the narrow concepts, use Phyla sp. or P. nodiflora sensu lato as appropriate with an explicit taxonomy note.

comparisons.key_distinctions: The best leaf split: P. nodiflora is usually widest beyond the middle and its teeth are concentrated in the distal half; P. lanceolata is widest nearer the middle and the teeth extend farther down the blade. Wedgeleaf frogfruit has a more distinctly wedge-shaped leaf architecture. Use several mature leaves rather than one odd leaf, because Phyla leaf shape varies along a shoot. Glandularia can also form low mats with verbena-like flowers, but its flowers are much larger and borne in more open terminal heads/spikes; Phyla has tiny flowers packed into a compact button/cylinder on a naked axillary peduncle.
comparisons.taxonomy_caution: Kew recognizes P. lanceolata and P. cuneifolia separately (checked 2026-10-19), whereas a 2025 peer-reviewed revision proposes including both within P. nodiflora s.l. Use the following leaf comparison as a traditional practical field heuristic, not a definitive taxonomic test. When several leaves overlap strongly, record Phyla sp. pending additional evidence.

field_matrix.focus: Multiple mature leaves, flowering head, leaf base
field_matrix.usual_pattern: Oblanceolate or spoon-shaped blade often broadest above its midpoint; teeth typically near distal half; lower blade narrows to an untoothed wedge.
field_matrix.limitation: Shape and teeth vary markedly, including within a shoot.

field_matrix.focus: Multiple mature leaves at similar nodes
field_matrix.usual_pattern: Often more elliptic/lanceolate and broadest around the middle, with teeth usually extending farther down the blade.
field_matrix.limitation: Broad overlap with P. nodiflora; 2025 revision treats this name within P. nodiflora s.l.

field_matrix.usual_pattern: Traditionally distinguished by relatively wedge-shaped, thicker or more leathery foliage.
field_matrix.limitation: Leaf shape and texture can overlap; 2025 revision treats this name within P. nodiflora s.l.

field_matrix.focus: Where flower stalk starts; flower size and head arrangement
field_matrix.usual_pattern: Larger individual flowers in terminal heads/spikes rather than many tiny flowers in an axillary stalked button.
field_matrix.limitation: Low growth habit and pinkish/white flowers alone are not distinguishing.

practical_groundcover_separators.frogfruit: many tiny white-to-lilac flowers around a purple/green button, on an axillary stalk
practical_groundcover_separators.other: small YELLOW composite daisy head, with ray/disk florets and involucral bracts; belongs to Asteraceae
practical_groundcover_separators.caution: both can be low, spreading and have toothed leaves; mat habit and opposite leaves alone do not settle it.

practical_groundcover_separators.frogfruit: usually longer wedge-based toothed leaves with a conspicuous flowering head
practical_groundcover_separators.other: rounded/kidney-shaped leaves with little or no obvious serration; flowers inconspicuous and solitary
practical_groundcover_separators.caution: nonflowering shoots need careful leaf inspection

practical_groundcover_separators.frogfruit: minute blooms in a very compact axillary button or cylinder
practical_groundcover_separators.other: larger showier clustered flowers; prairie verbena can have deeply dissected leaves, unlike the simple toothed blades of frogfruit
practical_groundcover_separators.caution: not all Glandularia leaves are equally divided; compare reproductive structures

practical_groundcover_separators.look_here_first: Examine the small white reproductive head and the length of mature leaves
practical_groundcover_separators.frogfruit: tiny distinct two-lipped flowers crowd a dark purplish/green compact spike; leaves shorter and often wedge-shaped
practical_groundcover_separators.other: a white ASTERACEAE composite head with many short ray and disk florets plus an involucre of green bracts; leaves typically narrow/longer and rough-hairy
practical_groundcover_separators.caution: both can sprawl or root at lower nodes and bear opposite toothed leaves. White color, root nodes or leaf arrangement alone do not separate them.

do_not_trust_alone: A single spoon-shaped leaf, as the traditionally separated Phyla names intergrade
The color or apparent number of blossoms in one cropped head
Mat-forming growth alone (multiple local groundcovers creep)
A cultivated or intentionally planted patch as evidence for local wild nativity
An older brown spike mistaken for an individual nutlet or seed
A visual claim of T-shaped hairs without genuine macro/microscope detail

visual_comparison.title: Frogfruit — trace the stalk, leaf edge, and tiny flower head
visual_comparison.subtitle: Crew field ID: first recognize the mat, then inspect actual flower and leaf structures. Two external Commons close-ups and one fruiting-head reference have image-level CC licenses and confirmed visible anatomy, but are not counted as physically installed canonical gallery files.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: First see a creeping mat. Then find the axillary, nearly leafless flower stalk and the many tiny flowers; use SEVERAL leaves, not just one, to evaluate the frogfruit type.

items.label: 1 — Low mat and repeated heads
items.image_role: Field habit / leaves and flowering stalks
items.caption: Look for the low mat, opposite leaves, and several upright slender stalks holding small heads. Rooting at the nodes is typical, but actual roots are not visible clearly enough in this photo to label.
items.why_it_matters: Establishes field context; neither a creeping mat nor a buttonlike head by itself establishes which Phyla species it is.
items.creator: Dinesh Valke

items.label: 2 — Flower parts and leaf teeth (arrows)
items.image_role: Actual upper leaf teeth, tiny flowers, and leafless head stalk
items.caption: The upper portions of the leaves have conspicuous teeth while their narrowed bases tend to be entire. Many tiny individual flowers occupy a compact purplish head on a mostly leafless peduncle (flower stalk). The labels identify directly visible structures, not unphotographed roots or microscopic hairs.
items.why_it_matters: Together the leaf arrangement and small axillary head help establish Phyla. Leaf width and where teeth start only suggest traditional P. nodiflora versus P. lanceolata; they are not decisive when traits overlap.
items.creator: yating
items.photo_status: INSTALLED_EXACT_SPECIES; PHOTO_INSPECTED_2026-10-19; guide species #58 credits yating CC BY-NC; standalone NONCOMMERCIAL display only; original JPEG unchanged and live arrow overlay added

items.label: 3 — More mature leaves and heads
items.image_role: Several older serrate leaves and rounded-to-elongated heads
items.caption: Check multiple leaves along the mat: broad upper blades, toothed distal margins, and narrower bases. The flower head may elongate as it matures. This photo is a second independent growth view, not a microscopic hair or fruit confirmation.
items.why_it_matters: Leaf shape is variable; verifying the pattern on more than one leaf is better than diagnosing a plant from its most unusual leaf.
items.creator: Forest & Kim Starr

items.label: 4 — Opposite leaves and real teeth (external licensed detail)
items.image_role: Opposite leaf pair, cuneate bases and toothed blade edges
items.caption: On this actual photo, a pair of leaves attaches opposite at a stem node. Their broad upper margins are toothed and the blades narrow toward the base. Good for training on leaf attachment, but the visible pattern cannot uniquely distinguish the currently separated Phyla taxa.
items.why_it_matters: Learn what an opposite node and distal serration actually look like, then repeat the check along several different leaves.
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.photo_status: EXTERNAL_REFERENCE_ONLY; Wikimedia source/original physically inspected via linked full-image view on 2026-10-19; license/photo ID verified; no canonical JPEG installed; no arrows

items.label: 5 — Surface texture and leaf teeth (external licensed detail)
items.image_role: Upper leaf surface and enlarged tooth placement
items.caption: This external close-up clearly resolves an upper leaf face, its midrib and multiple marginal teeth. Reflective white flecks are NOT evidence of visible individual T-shaped hairs; those require further magnification.
items.why_it_matters: Understand serrate versus entire blade sections at a useful field scale without pretending the hair anatomy was photographed.
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.photo_status: EXTERNAL_REFERENCE_ONLY; visually inspected original; license/photo ID verified; not installed; no arrows

items.label: 6 — An older fruiting spike (external licensed detail)
items.image_role: Mature elongating head among creeping leaves
items.caption: An older head is elongated and pale green with tightly overlapping scales/bracts. This is NOT an isolated mericarp image; dissect the head for the one-seeded fruit pieces.
items.why_it_matters: Shows how the same species looks different after the buttonlike flowering stage. Still need a true dissected fruit macro for advanced confirmation.
items.creator: Forest & Kim Starr
items.photo_status: EXTERNAL_REFERENCE_ONLY; visually inspected source image, Commons CC BY 3.0 verified; not installed as source JPEG; no arrows

items.label: 7 — Opposite nodes and fruiting spike attachment (licensed source photo)
items.image_role: Three mature opposite leaf pairs, nearly leafless axillary peduncles and elongated older flower/fruit heads
items.caption: Trace the central creeping stem. At each visible node a pair of toothed leaves sits opposite, and a slender flower-head stalk rises from a leaf axil. Each head is elongated/scaly as flowers age. No roots, isolated mericarps or individual T-shaped hairs are resolved in this image.
items.why_it_matters: This photograph puts the paired leaves, AXILLARY peduncle insertion and flowering-to-fruiting change together in one useful view. It is NOT a photograph proving roots at nodes.
